From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia

|  |  |
| --- | --- |
|  | This article needs to be **updated**. Please help update this article to reflect recent events or newly available information. *(March 2024)* |


[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/40/201812_Grateful_to_General_Secretary%2C_Endeavoring_to_a_New_Era_Slogan_in_Chun%27an.jpg/250px-201812_Grateful_to_General_Secretary%2C_Endeavoring_to_a_New_Era_Slogan_in_Chun%27an.jpg)](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:201812_Grateful_to_General_Secretary,_Endeavoring_to_a_New_Era_Slogan_in_Chun'an.jpg)

"Grateful to the General Secretary, Endeavoring towards a New Era", a [Big-character poster](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Big-character_poster "Big-character poster") slogan in Chun'an

A [cult of personality](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cult_of_personality "Cult of personality") has been developing around [Xi Jinping](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xi_Jinping "Xi Jinping") since he became [General Secretary](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/General_Secretary_of_the_Chinese_Communist_Party "General Secretary of the Chinese Communist Party") of the [Chinese Communist Party](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chinese_Communist_Party "Chinese Communist Party") (CCP) in 2012.[[1]](#cite_note-:2-1)

After [Deng Xiaoping](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deng_Xiaoping "Deng Xiaoping") started the [reform and opening up](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reform_and_opening_up "Reform and opening up") and introduced the concept of [collective leadership](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Collective_leadership "Collective leadership") in the late 1970s, there was no longer a cult of personality around Chinese leaders. Deng and others wanted to prevent another leader from rising above the party as [Mao Zedong](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mao_Zedong "Mao Zedong") had done.[[2]](#cite_note-:1-2) However, when Xi came to power in 2012, he started centralizing power and paved the way for a cult of personality.[[3]](#cite_note-:3-3)

The [Chinese Communist Party](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chinese_Communist_Party "Chinese Communist Party") (CCP) denies that there is any cult of personality around Xi. The CCP's rules explicitly forbid personality cults. Xie Chuntao, director of the government-funded Central Party School's academic department, claimed the "respect and love" ordinary Chinese felt for Xi was "natural" and "heartfelt" and bore no similarities to a cult of personality. He added that memories of the excesses of [Mao's cult](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mao_Zedong's_cult_of_personality "Mao Zedong's cult of personality") were strong enough that the CCP would not allow another leader to form a cult around himself.[[2]](#cite_note-:1-2)[[4]](#cite_note-4)

Since Xi assumed power in 2012, books, cartoons, pop songs and dance routines have honored his dictatorship.[[1]](#cite_note-:2-1)[[5]](#cite_note-5)[[3]](#cite_note-:3-3)[[6]](#cite_note-6)[[7]](#cite_note-7) In 2017, the local government of [Jiangxi province](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jiangxi "Jiangxi") told [Christians](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christianity_in_China "Christianity in China") to replace their pictures of [Jesus](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jesus "Jesus") with Xi Jinping.[[8]](#cite_note-8)[[9]](#cite_note-9)[[10]](#cite_note-10)

Writing in the *[Sydney Morning Herald](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Sydney_Morning_Herald "The Sydney Morning Herald")*, Philip Wen notes that "perhaps the most stunning characteristic shared with Mao has been a growing personality cult around Xi fanned by the central propaganda department, which has produced some jarring results: newspaper front-pages dominated by Xi's every move, saccharine music videos professing love and loyalty to the leader."[[11]](#cite_note-smh.com.au-11) In May 2016, just prior to the 50th anniversary celebration of [Mao](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mao "Mao")'s [Cultural Revolution](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cultural_Revolution "Cultural Revolution"), a "Mao-themed revival show" at the [Great Hall of the People](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Hall_of_the_People "Great Hall of the People") featuring revolutionary "red songs" was designed to generate nostalgia for the Mao era, with "giant images of Mao and Xi projected on stage."[[11]](#cite_note-smh.com.au-11)

In March 2017, Xi claimed that he carried bags of 110 kilograms of wheat over 3 miles of mountain road without changing shoulder,[[12]](#cite_note-12) a feat deemed extraordinary[[13]](#cite_note-chinadigitaltimes-13) and broadcast by [China Central Television](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/China_Central_Television "China Central Television") during what was described as an image-crafting campaign.[[13]](#cite_note-chinadigitaltimes-13)

When he was re-elected in 2017, Xi dominated the front page of the *[People's Daily](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/People's_Daily "People's Daily")*[[a]](#cite_note-14) compared to previous editions, which emphasized a "collective leadership" model.[[14]](#cite_note-15)

The political ideology bearing his name, [Xi Jinping Thought](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xi_Jinping_Thought "Xi Jinping Thought"), was enshrined into the CCP's constitution in the [19th National Congress](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/19th_National_Congress_of_the_Chinese_Communist_Party "19th National Congress of the Chinese Communist Party") in October 2017[[15]](#cite_note-16) and into the [state constitution](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Constitution_of_China "Constitution of China") in 2018.[[16]](#cite_note-17) [China Central Television](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/China_Central_Television "China Central Television") (CCTV) also showed members of the [National People's Congress](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_People's_Congress "National People's Congress") "crying in happiness" because of Xi Jinping's [re-election as president in 2018](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/13th_National_People's_Congress "13th National People's Congress").[[17]](#cite_note-:0-18)

Since October 2017, many universities across China have placed Xi Jinping Thought at the core of their curricula, the first time since Mao Zedong that a Chinese leader has been accorded similar academic stature.[[18]](#cite_note-19) [Fudan University](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fudan_University "Fudan University") revised their charter to remove "academic independence and freedom of thought" and include a "pledge to follow the Communist party's leadership", leading to protests among the students.[[19]](#cite_note-20)[[20]](#cite_note-21) It also said that Fudan University had to "equip its teachers and employees" with Xi Jinping Thought, leading to concerns about the diminishing academic freedom of Fudan.[[21]](#cite_note-22)[[22]](#cite_note-23)

Xi's cult of personality has been especially pronounced in Xinjiang.[[23]](#cite_note-24) Former inmates in the [Xinjiang internment camps](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xinjiang_internment_camps "Xinjiang internment camps") claimed that they were forced to give thanks to the leader by chanting "[Long live](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wansui "Wansui") Xi Jinping."[[24]](#cite_note-25)

In October 2018, [Hunan TV](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hunan_Television "Hunan Television") started airing a game show about Xi Jinping and his ideology.[[25]](#cite_note-26) In January 2019, [Alibaba](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alibaba_Group "Alibaba Group") released a [mobile app](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mobile_app "Mobile app") for studying Xi Jinping Thought named *[Xuexi Qiangguo](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xuexi_Qiangguo "Xuexi Qiangguo")*. (The name of the app is a [pun](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homophonic_puns_in_Standard_Chinese "Homophonic puns in Standard Chinese") on Xi Jinping's name. *Xuéxí* can mean "learning" or "learn from Xi.")[[26]](#cite_note-27)[[27]](#cite_note-28) As of October 2019, it had more than 100 million active users,[[28]](#cite_note-29) and is now claimed to be the most downloaded item on Apple's domestic App Store, surpassing social media apps such as [WeChat](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/WeChat "WeChat") and [TikTok](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/TikTok "TikTok") (also known as Douyin in Mandarin).[[29]](#cite_note-30)

Apps such as Toutiao, Tencent, and Sina have been forced to use what has been described as "a super algorithm", where the story at the top "has to be about Xi".[[30]](#cite_note-31)[[31]](#cite_note-32)

In October 2017, the [CCP Politburo](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Politburo_of_the_Chinese_Communist_Party "Politburo of the Chinese Communist Party") named Xi Jinping *[lingxiu](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lingxiu_(disambiguation) "Lingxiu (disambiguation)")* ([领袖](https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/%E9%A2%86%E8%A2%96 "wikt:领袖")), a reverent term for "leader" and a title previously only given to [Chiang Kai-shek](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chiang_Kai-shek "Chiang Kai-shek"), Mao Zedong, and his immediate successor, [Hua Guofeng](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hua_Guofeng "Hua Guofeng").[[32]](#cite_note-33)[[33]](#cite_note-34)[[34]](#cite_note-35) He is also sometimes called the "[Great Helmsman](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Helmsman_(disambiguation) "Great Helmsman (disambiguation)")" (大舵手),[[17]](#cite_note-:0-18) and in July 2018, [Li Zhanshu](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Li_Zhanshu "Li Zhanshu"), the [Chairman of the Standing Committee of the National People's Congress](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chairman_of_the_Standing_Committee_of_the_National_People's_Congress "Chairman of the Standing Committee of the National People's Congress"), referred to Xi as the "[eternal core](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leadership_core "Leadership core")" of the party.[[35]](#cite_note-36) On 25 December 2019, the politburo officially named Xi as "People's Leader" (人民领袖; *rénmín lǐngxiù*), a title only Mao held previously.[[36]](#cite_note-37)

From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia

The **Belt and Road Forum for International Cooperation** (also known as the **Belt and Road Forum** or **BRFIC**)[[1]](#cite_note-par-1) is an international political and economic forum of the [Belt and Road Initiative](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Belt_and_Road_Initiative "Belt and Road Initiative").

The forum will be a platform for working out action plans for implementation of the initiative in the areas of infrastructure, energy and resources, production capacity, [trade](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_the_largest_trading_partners_of_China "List of the largest trading partners of China") and investment and identification of major projects.[[2]](#cite_note-event-2) It is also intended to be an opportunity for the signing of cooperation agreements with countries and international organizations in the areas of financial cooperation mechanism; a cooperation platform for science, technology and environmental protection; and enhanced exchanges and training of talent and financing agreements for backing projects.[[2]](#cite_note-event-2)

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/d8/Before_the_beginning_of_the_Belt_and_Road_international_forum.jpg/250px-Before_the_beginning_of_the_Belt_and_Road_international_forum.jpg)](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Before_the_beginning_of_the_Belt_and_Road_international_forum.jpg)

Participants of the 1st Belt and Road Forum held in 2017

The first event was on 14 and 15 May 2017 in Beijing, and drew 29 foreign heads of state and government and representatives from more than 130 countries and 70 international organizations.[[3]](#cite_note-3)[[4]](#cite_note-list-4)

The purpose of the forum is described by Wang Xiaotao, deputy head of the [National Development and Reform Commission](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Development_and_Reform_Commission "National Development and Reform Commission"), in an interview with Xinhua as building "a more open and efficient international cooperation platform; a closer, stronger partnership network; and to push for a more just, reasonable and balanced international governance system."[[2]](#cite_note-event-2) [Western media](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Western_media "Western media") coverage portrayed the forum in a similar way with [CNN](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CNN "CNN") referring to the event under the headline "China's new world order" and the *[Los Angeles Times](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Los_Angeles_Times "Los Angeles Times")* running the article "Globalization 2.0: How China's two-day summit aims to shape a new world order".[[5]](#cite_note-cnn-5)[[6]](#cite_note-latimes-6)

A second Belt and Road Forum was held from 25 to 27 April 2019 in Beijing.[[1]](#cite_note-par-1) Thirty-seven heads of state attended the second BRFIC, as did about five thousand other representatives.[[7]](#cite_note-7)

The second forum identified 283 projects, agreements, or initiatives proceeding under the BRI.[[8]](#cite_note-:32-8): 60

During the second forum, China's [Ministry of Ecology and Environment](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ministry_of_Ecology_and_Environment "Ministry of Ecology and Environment") established the BRI International Green Development Coalition as a joint project with the environmental agencies of twenty-five other countries.[[8]](#cite_note-:32-8): 60

A third forum was held from 17 to 19 October 2023.[[9]](#cite_note-9)

From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia

**Islamophobia in the People's Republic of China** refers to the set of discourses, behaviors and structures which express feelings of anxiety, fear, hostility and rejection towards [Islam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Islam "Islam") and/or [Muslims in China](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Islam_in_China "Islam in China").

Negative views and attitudes towards Muslims in China are widespread, and some Muslim communities in China face legal restrictions on their ability to practice.[[1]](#cite_note-:1-1) Muslim prisoners in detention centers and internment camps have faced practices such as being [force-fed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Force-feeding "Force-feeding") pork.[[2]](#cite_note-:4-2) Prohibitions on [fasting during Ramadan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fasting_during_Ramadan "Fasting during Ramadan") for [Uyghurs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uyghurs "Uyghurs") in [Xinjiang](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xinjiang "Xinjiang") are couched in terms of protecting residents' [free will](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Free_will "Free will").[[3]](#cite_note-3)

In the 21st century, coverage of Muslims in Chinese media has generally been negative,[[4]](#cite_note-:5-4) and Islamophobic content is widespread on Chinese social media.[[5]](#cite_note-:6-5) Anti-Muslim attitudes in China have been tied to both narratives regarding historical conflicts between China and Muslim polities as well as contemporary rhetoric related to terrorism in China and abroad.[[6]](#cite_note-:7-6)[[7]](#cite_note-7)

Recent scholars contend that historical conflicts between the Han Chinese and Muslims like the [Dungan Revolt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dungan_Revolt_(1862%E2%80%931877) "Dungan Revolt (1862–1877)") against the [Qing dynasty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Qing_dynasty "Qing dynasty") have been used by some Han Chinese to legitimize and fuel anti-Muslim beliefs and bias in contemporary China.[[6]](#cite_note-:7-6)[[8]](#cite_note-8) Following the [establishment of the People's Republic of China](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Establishment_of_the_People's_Republic_of_China "Establishment of the People's Republic of China") in 1949, ten ethnic groups that were traditionally Muslim eventually were designated as part of the [state's recognized ethnicities](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_ethnic_groups_in_China "List of ethnic groups in China").[[9]](#cite_note-:8-9) According to [Emily Feng](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emily_Feng "Emily Feng"), state-sanctioned ethnic distinctions for traditionally Muslim groups created a "buffer against proselytization and the further spread of Islam in China."[[9]](#cite_note-:8-9) Scholars and researchers have also argued that Western Islamophobia and the "[war on terror](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/War_on_terror "War on terror")" have contributed to the mainstreaming of anti-Muslim sentiments and practices in China.[[10]](#cite_note-10)[[11]](#cite_note-11)[[12]](#cite_note-12)

Middle Easterners in China interviewed by the [Middle East Institute](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Middle_East_Institute "Middle East Institute") in 2018 generally did not report discrimination. However, a Yemeni student said that he received unfavorable reactions from some Chinese when he stated he was a Muslim.[[13]](#cite_note-13)

It has been reported that Muslims were being forced to eat pork in detention centers and in the [Xinjiang internment camps](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xinjiang_internment_camps "Xinjiang internment camps").[[2]](#cite_note-:4-2) Since [Xi Jinping](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xi_Jinping "Xi Jinping") became [General Secretary of the Chinese Communist Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/General_Secretary_of_the_Chinese_Communist_Party "General Secretary of the Chinese Communist Party"), campaigns against Islam have extended to the [Hui people](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hui_people "Hui people") and [Utsul](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Utsul "Utsul") community in Hainan.[[14]](#cite_note-14)[[15]](#cite_note-15)[[16]](#cite_note-16)[[1]](#cite_note-:1-1) In 2017, the Chinese government officially prohibited Muslims in Xinjiang from naming their babies "Muhammad" among other Islamic names.[[17]](#cite_note-17)[[18]](#cite_note-18) In 2023, [NPR](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NPR "NPR") reported on ways that the [Chinese government](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Government_of_China "Government of China") is actively preventing Chinese Muslim from going on the [Hajj](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hajj "Hajj") such as confiscation of passports.[[19]](#cite_note-19) In [Uyghur](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uyghurs "Uyghurs") communities, Islamic education for children has been prohibited and teaching the [Quran](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quran "Quran") to children has resulted in criminal prosecution.[[20]](#cite_note-20)[[21]](#cite_note-21)[[22]](#cite_note-22)[[23]](#cite_note-23) In 2023, government efforts to "[sinicize](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sinicization "Sinicization")" a mosque in [Yunnan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yunnan "Yunnan") by destroying its minaret and dome roof led to clashes with worshippers.[[24]](#cite_note-24)

China supports United Nations programs to combat Islamophobia.[[25]](#cite_note-:13-25): 69 China highlights its contributions to these UN endeavors in its diplomatic discourse opposing the [Clash of Civilizations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clash_of_Civilizations "Clash of Civilizations") thesis.[[25]](#cite_note-:13-25): 68

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/9a/Front_gate_of_Ximen_Mosque%2C_Dali.jpg/250px-Front_gate_of_Ximen_Mosque%2C_Dali.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Front_gate_of_Ximen_Mosque,_Dali.jpg)

Mosque with dome removed due to [Sinicization](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sinicization "Sinicization") policy

Traditional media in China were used to be very cautious on the coverage of ethnic issues—particularly Muslim issues, to foster a positive environment both for solidarity among China's different ethnic groups and religions and China's diplomatic relations with Muslim countries. Starting in 2015, hostility towards Muslims and Islam surged after series of terrorist attacks and the emergence of the [European refugee crisis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_refugee_crisis "European refugee crisis").[[26]](#cite_note-26) Some observers contend that although negative stereotypes about Muslims have long existed in China, a global rise of Islamophobia, the influence of fake news, and the actions of the Chinese government towards their Muslim minorities have exacerbated Islamophobia in the country.[[27]](#cite_note-:3-27)

US-based researchers [Rose Luqiu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/L%C3%BCqiu_Luwei "Lüqiu Luwei") and Fan Yang contend in *[The Washington Post](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Washington_Post "The Washington Post")* that anti-Muslim sentiment has been spurred by Chinese news reports, which tend to portray Muslims as prone to terrorism, or as recipients of disproportionate aid from the government.[[28]](#cite_note-28) A 2018 study by the two researchers found that Chinese news coverage of Muslims and Islam was generally negative. The study found that non-Muslim Chinese hold negative views towards Islam and Muslims, and that some Chinese Muslims report discrimination and awareness of negative portrayals of themselves in the media.[[4]](#cite_note-:5-4)

The same two researchers analyzed over 10,000 posts on Weibo in 2019 relating to Islam and found that anti-Muslim sentiment was a common frame. Chinese Muslims users on the site reported that they faced challenges in attempting to have others understand their faith, due to the prevailing Han-centric discourse and government censorship.[[29]](#cite_note-29)

On 21 June 2023, 31 people died and seven others were injured at the Fuyang Barbecue Restaurant ([Chinese](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simplified_Chinese_characters "Simplified Chinese characters"): 富洋烧烤店) in [Xingqing District](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xingqing_District "Xingqing District"), [Yinchuan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yinchuan "Yinchuan"), [Ningxia Hui Autonomous Region](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ningxia_Hui_Autonomous_Region "Ningxia Hui Autonomous Region"), China, after a gas explosion occurred on the eve of the [Dragon Boat Festival](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dragon_Boat_Festival "Dragon Boat Festival").

The [explosion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Explosion "Explosion") was the deadliest in China since 2019, when 78 died in [a blast](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2019_Xiangshui_chemical_plant_explosion "2019 Xiangshui chemical plant explosion") at a chemical plant in the eastern province of [Jiangsu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jiangsu "Jiangsu").[[2]](#cite_note-2)

According to the state broadcaster [China Central Television](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/China_Central_Television "China Central Television") (CCTV), the explosion occurred at around 8:40 p.m. local time on a busy street, following a leak of a [liquefied petroleum gas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liquefied_petroleum_gas "Liquefied petroleum gas") tank inside the kitchen of the restaurant.[[3]](#cite_note-3)[[4]](#cite_note-4)[[5]](#cite_note-bbcnews-5)[[6]](#cite_note-NOS-6) Authorities are investigating the exact cause of the leak.[[6]](#cite_note-NOS-6)[*[needs update](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Manual_of_Style/Dates_and_numbers#Chronological_items "Wikipedia:Manual of Style/Dates and numbers")*]

Over a dozen firefighters battled the blaze while smoke billowed from a large opening in the front of the restaurant. The street was strewn with shards of glass and other debris.[[7]](#cite_note-7) The [Ministry of Emergency Management](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ministry_of_Emergency_Management "Ministry of Emergency Management") said that more than 100 personnel and 20 vehicles from fire and rescue services were deployed to the location.[[5]](#cite_note-bbcnews-5) A video from the social media platform [Douyin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Douyin "Douyin") showed first responders with ladders, attempting to reach victims that were trapped on the second floor.[[8]](#cite_note-8)

At least 31 people died in the explosion, with seven others injured.[[5]](#cite_note-bbcnews-5) The casualties included high school students and retirees. Of those killed, many died by [smoke inhalation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Smoke_inhalation "Smoke inhalation").[[9]](#cite_note-9)

The provincial government relocated 64 families from neighboring residential compounds to hotels.[[10]](#cite_note-China_Daily-10)

Local media reported that based on an initial inquiry by the [fire department](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fire_department "Fire department"), an employee at the restaurant detected the odor of a [gas leak](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gas_leak "Gas leak") approximately one hour prior to the explosion. Subsequently, the employee identified a damaged valve on a liquefied gas tank and was in the midst of replacing it when the blast occurred.[[5]](#cite_note-bbcnews-5) Nine people, including the restaurant's owner, shareholders, and staff were held by police following the explosion while their financial assets were ordered frozen.[[11]](#cite_note-11)

Yinchuan city government holds a press conference on the explosion.

General Secretary of the Communist Party [Xi Jinping](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xi_Jinping "Xi Jinping") urged for utmost efforts in providing medical care to the injured.[[12]](#cite_note-12)[[13]](#cite_note-13) He ordered an "all-out rescue and treatment of the injured" and requested strengthened safety measures.[[14]](#cite_note-14)

On 22 June 2023, Yinchuan authorities vowed to launch an investigation into relevant industries to avoid similar calamities in the future.[[10]](#cite_note-China_Daily-10)

Since 2014, the [government of the People's Republic of China](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Government_of_the_People's_Republic_of_China "Government of the People's Republic of China") has committed a series of ongoing [human rights abuses](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Human_rights#Violations "Human rights") against [Uyghurs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uyghurs "Uyghurs") and other [Turkic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Turkic_peoples "Turkic peoples") Muslim minorities in [Xinjiang](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xinjiang "Xinjiang") which has often been characterized as [persecution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Persecution "Persecution") or as [genocide](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Genocide "Genocide"). There have been reports of mass [arbitrary arrests and detention](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arbitrary_arrest_and_detention "Arbitrary arrest and detention"), [torture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Torture "Torture"), [mass surveillance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mass_surveillance "Mass surveillance"), cultural and religious persecution, [family separation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Family_separation "Family separation"), [forced labor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Forced_labor "Forced labor"), [sexual violence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sexual_violence "Sexual violence"), and violations of [reproductive rights](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reproductive_rights "Reproductive rights").

In 2014, the [administration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xi_Jinping_Administration "Xi Jinping Administration") of [Chinese Communist Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chinese_Communist_Party "Chinese Communist Party") (CCP) [general secretary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/General_Secretary_of_the_Chinese_Communist_Party "General Secretary of the Chinese Communist Party") [Xi Jinping](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xi_Jinping "Xi Jinping") launched the [Strike Hard Campaign Against Violent Terrorism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Strike_Hard_Campaign_Against_Violent_Terrorism "Strike Hard Campaign Against Violent Terrorism"), which involved surveillance and restrictions in Xinjiang. Beginning in 2017, under [Xinjiang Party secretary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Party_Secretary_of_Xinjiang "Party Secretary of Xinjiang") [Chen Quanguo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chen_Quanguo "Chen Quanguo"),[[2]](#cite_note-Khatchadourian-5-4-2021-2) the government incarcerated over an estimated one million Uyghurs without [legal process](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Legal_process "Legal process") in [internment camps](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xinjiang_internment_camps "Xinjiang internment camps") officially described as "vocational education and training centers", in the largest mass internment of an ethnic-religious minority group since [World War II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_War_II "World War II").[[3]](#cite_note-Finley-2020-3)[[4]](#cite_note-4) China began to wind down the camps in 2019, and some detainees were transferred to the [penal system](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Penal_system_in_China "Penal system in China"), while others were transferred to [forced labor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Forced_labor "Forced labor") and factory work programs.[[5]](#cite_note-5)[[6]](#cite_note-6)

In addition to mass detention, government policies have included suppression of Uyghur [religious practices](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Islam_in_China "Islam in China"),[[7]](#cite_note-7) political [indoctrination](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indoctrination "Indoctrination"),[[8]](#cite_note-reut_Musl-8) [forced sterilization](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Forced_sterilization "Forced sterilization"),[[9]](#cite_note-apne_Chin-9) forced [contraception](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Contraception "Contraception"),[[10]](#cite_note-10)[[11]](#cite_note-genocide_against_the_Uyghurs-11) and [forced abortion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Forced_abortion "Forced abortion").[[12]](#cite_note-urlwww.dw.com-12)[[13]](#cite_note-bbc-13) An estimated 16,000 [mosques](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mosque "Mosque") have been razed or damaged,[[2]](#cite_note-Khatchadourian-5-4-2021-2) and hundreds of thousands of children have been forcibly separated from their parents and sent to [boarding schools](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boarding_schools_in_China "Boarding schools in China").[[14]](#cite_note-2018FTFamily-14)[[15]](#cite_note-:1-15) Since 2017, preferential [family planning exemptions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Family_planning_policies_of_China#Ethnic_minority_policies "Family planning policies of China") previously available to Uyghurs have reportedly been reduced or removed.[[16]](#cite_note-:11-16)[[17]](#cite_note-:10-17) Chinese government statistics reported that from 2015 to 2018, [birth rates](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Birth_rate "Birth rate") in the mostly Uyghur regions of [Hotan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hotan "Hotan") and [Kashgar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kashgar "Kashgar") fell by more than 60%.[[9]](#cite_note-apne_Chin-9) In the same period, the national birth rate decreased by 9.7%.[[18]](#cite_note-data_Birt-18) According to *CNN*, Chinese authorities acknowledged that birth rates dropped by almost a third in 2018 in Xinjiang, but denied reports of forced sterilization.[[19]](#cite_note-cnn-fax-19) Birth rates in Xinjiang fell a further 24% in 2019, compared to a nationwide decrease of 4.2%.[[9]](#cite_note-apne_Chin-9)

The Chinese government denies having committed human rights abuses in Xinjiang.[[3]](#cite_note-Finley-2020-3)[[20]](#cite_note-20) International reactions have varied, with its actions being described as the [forced assimilation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Forced_assimilation "Forced assimilation") of Xinjiang, as [ethnocide](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ethnocide "Ethnocide") or [cultural genocide](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cultural_genocide "Cultural genocide"),[[21]](#cite_note-indy-21)[[22]](#cite_note-22) or as genocide. Those accusing China of genocide point to intentional acts they say violate [Article II of the Genocide Convention](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Genocide_Convention#Definition_of_genocide "Genocide Convention"),[[23]](#cite_note-BBC_News-2021-23)[[24]](#cite_note-icij_Brit-24)[[25]](#cite_note-Piotrowicz-25) which prohibits "acts committed with intent to destroy, in whole or in part", a "racial or religious group" including "causing serious bodily or mental harm to members of the group" and "measures intended to prevent births within the group".[[26]](#cite_note-Convention-text-26)

At the United Nations, several countries, predominantly in North America and Europe, signed letters condemning China's policies. On the other hand, several countries, predominantly in Asia and Africa, signed letters supporting the policies as an effort to combat terrorism in the region.[[27]](#cite_note-:53-27)[[28]](#cite_note-28)[[29]](#cite_note-29) In 2020, a case brought to the [International Criminal Court](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Criminal_Court "International Criminal Court") was dismissed because China is not a party to the [Rome Statute](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rome_Statute "Rome Statute"), meaning the ICC could not investigate them.[[30]](#cite_note-:0-30) I

Large-scale [protests](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Protest_and_dissent_in_China "Protest and dissent in China") and incidents of [civil disobedience](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Civil_disobedience "Civil disobedience") in the [People's Republic of China](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/People's_Republic_of_China "People's Republic of China") are described by [its government](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Government_of_China "Government of China") as "**mass incidents**" ([Chinese](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simplified_Chinese_characters "Simplified Chinese characters"): 群体性事件).[[1]](#cite_note-zonaeuropa-1)[[2]](#cite_note-china-org-cn-2)

The [Chinese government](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chinese_government "Chinese government") broadly defines mass incidents as "planned or impromptu gathering[s] that form because of internal contradictions", and may include public speeches or demonstrations, physical clashes, public airings of grievances, and other group behaviors that are seen as disrupting social stability.[[3]](#cite_note-3) Through contemporary analysis of such events four key aspects of mass incidents have been identified "diversified participants, highly organized actions, easily escalated conflicts and thornier disputes to settle".[[4]](#cite_note-:0-4) Mass incidents have occurred in China because of the treatment of workers within [state-owned enterprises](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/State-owned_enterprises_of_China "State-owned enterprises of China") (SOEs) and [special economic zones](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Special_economic_zones_of_China "Special economic zones of China") (SEZs), the widening of [income disparities](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Income_inequality_in_China "Income inequality in China"), and issues associated with development projects, namely forced land acquisition and environmental degradation.

Within the past few decades, the number of mass incidents occurring in China has seen significant growth, indicated by The Annual Report of China's Rules (2009).[[5]](#cite_note-:1-5) In more recent times the numbers have continued to be high yet are less documented making reliable statistics rare, however it is definite that the frequency of mass incidents has increased.[[4]](#cite_note-:0-4)

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/88/Graph_of_Number_of_Mass_Incidents_in_China.jpg/250px-Graph_of_Number_of_Mass_Incidents_in_China.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Graph_of_Number_of_Mass_Incidents_in_China.jpg)

Graph depicts the number of mass incidents that occurred in China from 1993 to 2006.[[4]](#cite_note-:0-4)

Mass incidents in China have been commonplace since the country's step towards socioeconomic transformation in the late 1970s, with incidents, described by Jiuchang Wei, as following this push for change like an "inseparable shadow".[[6]](#cite_note-6)

Mass incidents are characterized as any form of public disturbance. This includes any type of protesting, demonstrating, picketing as well as group petitioning.[[7]](#cite_note-:3-7) Those who are common participants in mass incidents include peasants, urban residents as well as workers within state-owned enterprises (SOEs) and special economic zones (SEZs).[[7]](#cite_note-:3-7) Numbers of those involved can range from tens to thousands. The behaviors associated with mass incidents differ, some are peaceful, involving petitions, appeal to authorities for aid as well as collective walks and sit ins.[[5]](#cite_note-:1-5)

Typically, there is a pattern to the collective behavior of mass incidents, with those occurring in rural areas to be of the more extreme nature than those in urban settings.[[5]](#cite_note-:1-5) This is because of less government involvement in country areas, meaning incidents have to reach severe levels for any intervention to occur.[[5]](#cite_note-:1-5) Despite this, city outbreaks of mass incidents are regarded as more serious, owing to the extreme effect they have on the government's image.[[5]](#cite_note-:1-5) Therefore, these areas are more controlled, in an attempt to prevent extreme behavior from occurring.[[5]](#cite_note-:1-5)

The 2000s saw the height of social unrest within China, marked by the outbreak of numerous mass incidents.[[8]](#cite_note-8) This was because of immense economic, social and political issues which arose from much development within China. Each of these issues have caused misgoverning within policies surrounding the treatment of China's citizens, within areas of labor, development projects and legal systems.[[9]](#cite_note-:2-9)

### Layoffs and abuse of workers

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Mass_incidents_in_China&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Layoffs and abuse of workers")]

The experiences of the SOE workers were mirrored within the [special economic zones](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Special_economic_zones_of_China "Special economic zones of China") (SEZs). However, workers within SEZs possessed very limited understanding of labor rights because the workforce mainly consisted of uneducated female migrants from poor rural areas.[[7]](#cite_note-:3-7) This meant the workers were less likely to revolt despite suffering appalling conditions.[[7]](#cite_note-:3-7) A set of data from 1992 of the [Guangdong](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guangdong "Guangdong") province reported on the high death rate of workers and the presence of over 500,000 child laborers and 2003 data stated that a third of SEZ workers received less than minimum wage.[[11]](#cite_note-11) In 2004 these issues reached their height and with a combination of labor shortages and a growing understanding of rights led to the outbreak of mass incidents. This included 863 protests across the Guangdong province.[[7]](#cite_note-:3-7) These protests involved over 50,000 workers and involved rioting over requests for higher pay and violence due to unpaid wages.[[7]](#cite_note-:3-7)

### Development projects

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Mass_incidents_in_China&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Development projects")]

Development projects are one of the main causes of mass incidents as they result in forced land requisition and environmental degradation. This seizure of land leaves homeowners and farmers facing eviction and loss of farmland.[[7]](#cite_note-:3-7) Many of these citizens attempt to dispute these projects, claiming they were neither sufficiently compensated nor consulted. Because the government ignored these complaints, the citizens resorted to public demonstrations.[[12]](#cite_note-:10-12) In 2003 and 2004 [forcible evictions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Forced_evictions_in_China "Forced evictions in China") became the reasoning behind a quarter of mass incidents, thus becoming one of the largest sources of civil dissent.[[7]](#cite_note-:3-7) This trend continued into 2013, with the highest quantity of mass incidents occurring because of land acquisition and housing demolition.[[4]](#cite_note-:0-4)

| [Christianity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christianity "Christianity") (mostly [Protestant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Protestantism_in_China "Protestantism in China") and [Catholic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Catholic_Church_in_China "Catholic Church in China")) | |

[Christianity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christianity "Christianity") has been present in [China](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/China "China") since the early medieval period, and became a significant presence in the country during the [early modern era](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Early_modern_era "Early modern era"). The [Church of the East](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Church_of_the_East "Church of the East") appeared in China in the 7th century, during the [Tang dynasty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tang_dynasty "Tang dynasty"). But it did not take root in China until its [reintroduction by the Jesuits](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jesuit_missions_in_China "Jesuit missions in China") during the 16th century.[[2]](#cite_note-2) Beginning in the early 19th century, [Protestant missions in China](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Protestant_missions_in_China "Protestant missions in China") attracted small but influential followings, and independent Chinese churches were also established.

Accurate data on Chinese Christians is difficult to access.[[3]](#cite_note-Hackett-3) There were around 4 million Christians before 1949 (3 million Catholics and 1 million Protestants).[[4]](#cite_note-4) The number of Chinese Christians had increased significantly since the easing of restrictions on religious activities during the [reform and opening up](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reform_and_opening_up "Reform and opening up") of the late 1970s.[[3]](#cite_note-Hackett-3) In 2018, the [State Council Information Office](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/State_Council_Information_Office "State Council Information Office") declared that there are over 44 million Christians (38 million Protestants and 6 million Catholics) in China.[[5]](#cite_note-5) On the other hand, some international Christian organizations estimate that there are tens of millions more, who choose not to publicly identify as such.[[6]](#cite_note-Wieland,_2013._p._3-6) These estimations are controversial because the organizations which make them are often accused of deliberately inflating them.[[3]](#cite_note-Hackett-3)[[6]](#cite_note-Wieland,_2013._p._3-6)[[7]](#cite_note-auto-7)

For most of Chinese imperial history, religious practice was tightly controlled by the state. The [People's Republic of China](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/People's_Republic_of_China "People's Republic of China") also heavily regulates religion, and has increasingly implemented a policy of [sinicization](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sinicization "Sinicization") of Christianity since 2018.[[8]](#cite_note-:2-8) Chinese people over the age of 18 are only allowed to join Christian groups that are registered with one of three state-controlled bodies, the [Chinese Catholic Patriotic Association](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chinese_Catholic_Patriotic_Association "Chinese Catholic Patriotic Association"), the [China Christian Council](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/China_Christian_Council "China Christian Council"), or the Protestant [Three-Self Patriotic Movement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Three-Self_Patriotic_Movement "Three-Self Patriotic Movement").[[9]](#cite_note-9) However, many Chinese Christians are members of informal networks and [underground churches](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underground_church "Underground church"), often known as [house churches](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/House_church_(China) "House church (China)"). These began to proliferate during the 1950s when many Christians rejected the state-controlled bodies.[[10]](#cite_note-10) Members of house churches represent diverse theological traditions, and have been described as representing a "silent majority" of Chinese Christians.[[11]](#cite_note-11)

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/cb/People_lighting_candles_in_a_church.JPG/250px-People_lighting_candles_in_a_church.JPG)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:People_lighting_candles_in_a_church.JPG)

[Han Chinese](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Han_Chinese "Han Chinese") [Christians](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christians "Christians") lighting candles in a church in [Shunyi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shunyi,_Beijing "Shunyi, Beijing"), [Beijing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beijing "Beijing").

There are various names used for the Abrahamic God in the [Chinese language](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chinese_language "Chinese language"), the most prevalent of them is "[Shangdi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shangdi "Shangdi")" (上帝; 'Highest Emperor'), commonly used by both Protestants and non-Christians, and "*Tianzhu*" (天主; 'Lord of Heaven'), commonly used by Catholics. The word "Shen" (神), which is also used by Chinese Protestants, may also refer to deities or the generative powers of nature in the context of [Chinese traditional religion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chinese_traditional_religion "Chinese traditional religion"). In addition, Christians have historically adopted terms from the [Chinese classics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chinese_classics "Chinese classics") as references to God, such as 'Ruler' (主宰; *Zhǔzǎi*) and 'Creator' (造物主; *Zàowùzhǔ*).

Chinese terms for Christian denominations include "Protestantism" (基督教新教; *Jīdū jiào xīn jiào*; 'New Christian religion'), "Catholicism" (天主教; *Tiānzhǔ jiào*; 'Heavenly Lord religion'), and "[Eastern Orthodoxy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chinese_Orthodox_Church "Chinese Orthodox Church")" (东正教; 東正教; *Dōng zhèng jiào*). [Orthodox Christianity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eastern_Orthodoxy "Eastern Orthodoxy") as a whole is referred to as *Zhèng jiào* (正教). Christians in China are referred to as 'Christ followers' (基督徒; *Jīdū tú*) or 'Christ religion followers' (基督教徒; *Jīdū jiào tú*).

The significant lack of evidence of Christianity's existence in China between the 3rd century and the 7th century can likely be attributed to the barriers which were placed in Persia by the [Sassanids](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sassanids "Sassanids") and the closure of the trade route in [Turkestan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Turkestan "Turkestan").[*[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")*][*[further explanation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Please_clarify "Wikipedia:Please clarify")*]

Both events prevented Christians from staying in contact with their mother church, the Syriac [Antiochian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antiochian "Antiochian") Church, thereby halting the spread of Christianity until the reign of [Emperor Taizong of Tang](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emperor_Taizong_of_Tang "Emperor Taizong of Tang") (627–649). Taizong, who had studied the Christian Scriptures which were given to him by the [Assyrian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Assyrian_people "Assyrian people") missionary [Alopen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alopen "Alopen"), realized "their propriety and truth and specifically ordered their preaching and transmission."[[12]](#cite_note-12)

> His virtues have been made manifest to you, and that unheard-of power over things, whether that which was openly exercised by Him or that which was used over the whole world by those who proclaimed Him: it has subdued the fires of passion, and caused races, and peoples, and nations most diverse in character to hasten with one accord to accept the same faith. For the deeds can be reckoned up and numbered which have been done in India, among the Seres [China], Persians, and Medes; in Arabia, Egypt, in Asia, Syria; among the Galatians, Parthians, Phrygians; in Achaia, Macedonia, Epirus; in all islands and provinces on which the rising and setting sun shines.

— [Arnobius](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arnobius "Arnobius") of Sicca, "Against the Heathen, Book II"

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/bf/Nestorians-1-.jpg/250px-Nestorians-1-.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Nestorians-1-.jpg)

The [Xi'an Stele](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xi'an_Stele "Xi'an Stele") was erected in 781, and documents 150 years of early Christian history in China.[[13]](#cite_note-hill-108-13) It includes texts both in [Chinese](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chinese_language "Chinese language") and in [Syriac](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Syriac_language "Syriac language").

[Li Keqiang](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Li_Keqiang "Li Keqiang"), former [premier of the People's Republic of China](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Premier_of_the_People's_Republic_of_China "Premier of the People's Republic of China") and member of the [17th](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/17th_Politburo_Standing_Committee_of_the_Chinese_Communist_Party "17th Politburo Standing Committee of the Chinese Communist Party"), [18th](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/18th_Politburo_Standing_Committee_of_the_Chinese_Communist_Party "18th Politburo Standing Committee of the Chinese Communist Party"), and [19th Politburo Standing Committee of the Chinese Communist Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/19th_Politburo_Standing_Committee_of_the_Chinese_Communist_Party "19th Politburo Standing Committee of the Chinese Communist Party"), died on 27 October 2023 at 00:10 CST in Shanghai, aged 68.[[1]](#cite_note-1)

Li Keqiang became the youngest Premier at the time of leaving office and the earliest to die among all Premiers since the 1949 [proclamation of the People's Republic of China](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Proclamation_of_the_People's_Republic_of_China "Proclamation of the People's Republic of China").[[2]](#cite_note-voanews2023-11-02-2)

### Resignations from party and governmental positions

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Death_of_Li_Keqiang&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Resignations from party and governmental positions")]

After the [first plenary session of the 20th Central Committee of the Chinese Communist Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_plenary_session_of_the_20th_Central_Committee_of_the_Chinese_Communist_Party "First plenary session of the 20th Central Committee of the Chinese Communist Party") in October 2022, Li resigned from his [party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chinese_Communist_Party "Chinese Communist Party") roles, including his membership of the Politburo Standing Committee. Following the first session of the [14th National People's Congress](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/14th_National_People's_Congress "14th National People's Congress"), he also stepped down as Premier, retiring from public office at the age of 67.

After his official retirement, Li maintained a low profile, did not participate in official affairs, and rarely appeared in public. On 30 August 2023, Li visited the [Mogao Caves](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mogao_Caves "Mogao Caves") in [Dunhuang, Gansu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dunhuang "Dunhuang"); this was his final public appearance.[[3]](#cite_note-3)

According to the 2010 biography *He Will Be China's Chief Steward: A Biography of Li Keqiang*, Li suffered from severe [myocarditis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Myocarditis "Myocarditis") during his time at [Peking University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peking_University "Peking University") due to overexertion. He frequently experienced [shortness of breath](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shortness_of_breath "Shortness of breath") during physically strenuous activities.[[4]](#cite_note-4)

Reports also indicated that Li had [diabetes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diabetes "Diabetes"), which was further exacerbated by his demanding domestic and diplomatic work.[[5]](#cite_note-voachinese.com-5) Cardiovascular and cerebrovascular diseases caused by [atherosclerosis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atherosclerosis "Atherosclerosis") is a common complication and leading cause of death among diabetes patients.[[6]](#cite_note-uptodate.com-6)

The *[South China Morning Post](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_China_Morning_Post "South China Morning Post")* reported that Li Keqiang had previously had [heart bypass](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coronary_artery_bypass_surgery "Coronary artery bypass surgery") surgery.[[7]](#cite_note-南华-7)

Li suffered a sudden heart attack while swimming at the *Shanghai Dongjiao Hotel* on 26 October 2023.[[7]](#cite_note-南华-7) He was accompanied by his wife [Cheng Hong](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cheng_Hong "Cheng Hong").[[8]](#cite_note-8) It was reported that the heart attack occurred around noon on 26 October. Li Keqiang was rushed to the Shanghai Shuguang Hospital (East Campus)[[9]](#cite_note-scmp.com-9) by security and medical personnel after the incident. All available resources were mobilized,[[10]](#cite_note-10) including top experts from Shanghai and the installation of an [extracorporeal membrane oxygenation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Extracorporeal_membrane_oxygenation "Extracorporeal membrane oxygenation") (ECMO) device that afternoon. Despite emergency rescue efforts lasting over 10 hours, medical teams were unable to save him. Li died at 12:10 a.m. the next day.

At 8:00 a.m. on 27 October, [China Central Television](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/China_Central_Television "China Central Television")'s program "Morning News" aired a brief announcement of the death of Li Keqiang, delivered by the host [Wang Yan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wang_Yang_(politician) "Wang Yang (politician)").[[11]](#cite_note-11) Subsequently, official media outlets, such as [Xinhua News Agency](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xinhua_News_Agency "Xinhua News Agency") and the China Central Television (CCTV) website, published identical official statements.[[12]](#cite_note-12)[[13]](#cite_note-13) Around 6:30 p.m., Xinhua News issued a formal condolence statement on behalf of the [Central Committee of the Chinese Communist Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Central_Committee_of_the_Chinese_Communist_Party "Central Committee of the Chinese Communist Party"), the [Standing Committee of the National People's Congress](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Standing_Committee_of_the_National_People's_Congress "Standing Committee of the National People's Congress"), the [State Council](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/State_Council_of_China "State Council of China"), and the [National Committee of the Chinese People's Political Consultative Conference](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Committee_of_the_Chinese_People's_Political_Consultative_Conference "National Committee of the Chinese People's Political Consultative Conference"). The statement referenced key political concepts, including the "[Two Establishes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Two_Establishes "Two Establishes")," "[Two Upholds](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Two_Upholds "Two Upholds")," "[Four Consciousnesses](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Four_Consciousnesses "Four Consciousnesses")," and "[Four Confidences](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Four_Confidences "Four Confidences")."[[14]](#cite_note-14) Later, at 7:00 p.m., the national news program [Xinwen Lianbo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xinwen_Lianbo "Xinwen Lianbo") positioned the announcement of condolences as the third news item, following coverage of activities involving current national leaders, including [General Secretary of the Chinese Communist Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/General_Secretary_of_the_Chinese_Communist_Party "General Secretary of the Chinese Communist Party") [Xi Jinping](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xi_Jinping "Xi Jinping") and Premier [Li Qiang](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Li_Qiang "Li Qiang"). This arrangement mirrored the reporting style used for the announcement of former Premier [Li Peng](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Li_Peng "Li Peng")'s death in 2019.[[15]](#cite_note-15)

### Relocation and viewing of the coffin

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Death_of_Li_Keqiang&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Relocation and viewing of the coffin")]

On the afternoon of 27 October, Li Keqiang's remains were transferred to Beijing from Shanghai aboard a special flight. Some roads were temporarily closed in Shanghai, with people along the route mourning.[[16]](#cite_note-16)[[9]](#cite_note-scmp.com-9) Upon arrival in Beijing, Li's remains was transferred to the [PLA General Hospital](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/301_Hospital "301 Hospital") in preparation for national mourning and funeral arrangements.[[17]](#cite_note-17)

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/fc/%E5%A4%A9%E5%AE%89%E9%97%A8%E7%AD%89%E5%9C%B0%E4%B8%8B%E5%8D%8A%E6%97%97%E6%82%BC%E5%BF%B5%E6%9D%8E%E5%85%8B%E5%BC%BA%E5%90%8C%E5%BF%97.webm/250px--%E5%A4%A9%E5%AE%89%E9%97%A8%E7%AD%89%E5%9C%B0%E4%B8%8B%E5%8D%8A%E6%97%97%E6%82%BC%E5%BF%B5%E6%9D%8E%E5%85%8B%E5%BC%BA%E5%90%8C%E5%BF%97.webm.jpg)](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/f/fc/%E5%A4%A9%E5%AE%89%E9%97%A8%E7%AD%89%E5%9C%B0%E4%B8%8B%E5%8D%8A%E6%97%97%E6%82%BC%E5%BF%B5%E6%9D%8E%E5%85%8B%E5%BC%BA%E5%90%8C%E5%BF%97.webm)

On 2 November 2023, Tiananmen Square, Xinhua Gate, the Great Hall of the People and the Ministry of Foreign Affairs all flew at half-mast to mourn Li Keqiang

On 2 November, national flags were flown at [half-mast](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Half-mast "Half-mast") at [Tiananmen Square](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tiananmen_Square "Tiananmen Square"), [Xinhua Gate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zhongnanhai "Zhongnanhai"), the [Great Hall of the People](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Hall_of_the_People "Great Hall of the People"), and the [Ministry of Foreign Affairs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ministry_of_Foreign_Affairs_(China) "Ministry of Foreign Affairs (China)"); at the headquarters of Party committees and governments of all [provinces](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Provinces_of_China "Provinces of China"), [autonomous regions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Autonomous_regions_of_China "Autonomous regions of China"), and [municipalities](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Direct-administered_municipality "Direct-administered municipality") directly under the central government; in the [special administrative regions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Special_administrative_regions_of_China "Special admi
